verdict.rationale: The pattern of command-form and infinitive verbs (the 'to do X' form) across Micah 6:8, Isaiah 1:17, Amos 5:24, James 1:27, and Matthew 23:23 places active care for the vulnerable in the slot of required covenant conduct, not optional benevolence. The Hebrew word 'justice' (mishpat, Strong's H4941) is the shared object of 'doing' in Micah and of 'seeking' in Isaiah, and Jesus glosses the equivalent triad as 'justice and mercy and faithfulness' (ten krisin kai to eleos kai ten pistin), calling them the weightier matters of the law. James assigns the participial acts of visiting orphans and widows to the predicate (the 'is' side of an equation sentence) of pure 'religion' (threskeia) before God. The duty reading holds across Hebrew prophecy, Synoptic gospel (the gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke that parallel each other), and Greek epistle (letter) with no material textual variant disturbing it. The Galatians 1:6-9 anchor governs gospel fidelity rather than social ethics, so it neither establishes nor undercuts the duty claim and is treated as a complicating, off-target text.

scripture.force: The verse states what YHWH (the covenant name of God) requires of man as a triad (three-part set) of infinitive constructs (the 'to do X' form) governed by the verb of demand: 'to do justice' (asot mishpat), 'love mercy' (chesed), and 'walk humbly'. The infinitive 'to do' (asot) places justice in the slot of obligated action, not sentiment. The Hebrew poetic structure pairs the lines in stepped lines, framing all three as the content of the divine requirement rather than as graded options.

A dense chain of imperatives (direct commands): 'learn to do good', 'seek justice' (dirshu mishpat), 'correct the oppressed' (chamots), 'defend' (shaphat) 'the orphan' (yathom), 'plead for the widow' (almanah). The ETCBC parse (a syntactic analysis of the Hebrew Bible from a Dutch research project) marks the verbs as Predicate (the action-side of the sentence) and the named vulnerable parties as Object (the 'who-is-acted-on' role), so the grammar makes the orphan (yathom) and widow (almanah) the direct objects of commanded action. The imperative mood (command form) removes the reading that this is descriptive rather than required.

Amos commands that 'justice' (mishpat) roll down like waters and 'righteousness' (tsedaqah) like an ever-flowing stream. The jussive verb form (a 'let it be done' command form) and the simile (a comparison using 'like') place justice (mishpat) and righteous-dealing (tsedaqah) as the demanded outcome of covenant life, set in direct contrast (Amos 5:21-23) with religious-ritual activity God refuses to accept. The same noun 'justice' (mishpat) that anchors Micah 6:8 and Isaiah 1:17 recurs here as the required content of Israel's life before God, widening the canon spread within the prophets.

Jesus rebukes scrupulous tithers for neglecting 'the weightier matters of the law' (ta barytera tou nomou), naming them 'justice and mercy and faithfulness' (ten krisin kai to eleos kai ten pistin). 'Justice' (krisis) and 'mercy' (eleos) are the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint, abbreviated LXX) renderings of the Hebrew 'justice' (mishpat) and 'mercy' (chesed), so Jesus directly endorses the Micah 6:8 triad as still binding and explicitly labels these as weightier than ceremonial precision. The construction is a contrastive parallel that affirms justice (krisis) and mercy (eleos) as required content of obedience.

'Pure' (kathara) and undefiled 'religion' (threskeia) before God is defined by an explanatory infinitive (a 'to-do' phrase that unpacks the meaning), 'to visit, look after' (episkeptesthai) 'orphans' (orphanous) and widows in their 'affliction' (thlipsis). The predicate nominative construction (a noun completing a 'X is Y' statement) equates acceptable religion (threskeia) with this active care, so the duty is built into the definition rather than appended as an example. The present infinitive (the 'ongoing to-do' form) signals ongoing, habitual attention rather than a single act.

Paul pronounces a 'curse' (anathema) on anyone who preaches a 'gospel' (euangelion) contrary to the one received. The lexical subject here is the content of the proclaimed gospel (euangelion) and the penalty for distorting it, not the ethics of caring for the poor. This anchor concerns gospel fidelity and is off the semantic axis (off the topic-line of word-meaning) of the social-duty proposition.

complicating_texts.resolution: The Galatians 1:6-9 anchor uses 'gospel' (euangelion) and 'curse' (anathema) to defend the integrity of the preached gospel (euangelion) against a different message. It does not address care for the poor, orphan, widow, or oppressed at the word-meaning level, so it cannot make social concern either a gospel essential or a denial. It is resolved as off-target and assigned supports=neutral, leaving the duty verdict to rest on Micah 6:8, Isaiah 1:17, Amos 5:24, Matthew 23:23, and James 1:27.

Some readers cite Jesus's saying 'these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others' (tauta edei poiesai kakeina me aphienai) as preserving the lesser duties, raising the question whether 'justice' (krisis) and 'mercy' (eleos) are merely co-required with ritual. The grammar makes them the weightier (barytera) matters by explicit predicate (the 'is' side of the sentence), so neglect of justice (krisis) and mercy (eleos) is the named hypocrisy regardless of ceremonial scruple, confirming the duty reading.

variants.note: Anchor verses are Old Testament prophecy (Micah 6:8, Isaiah 1:17, Amos 5:24), a Synoptic gospel saying (one of the parallel gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke; here Matthew 23:23), and a Catholic and a Pauline epistle (James 1:27, Galatians 1:6-9), none in the CBGM ECM (a computer-based method for evaluating New Testament manuscript variants, with its critical edition) scope for this run. The James 1:27 article-and-pronoun cluster (the 'the' and 'this/that' words) around the widow phrase carries minor manuscript variation but does not touch the orphan-and-widow care words that anchor the verdict. Matthew 23:23 has known minor variation in the order of the three weightier matters, but 'justice' (krisis) and 'mercy' (eleos) are stable across the tradition.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the prophetic 'justice and mercy' (mishpat and chesed) demands as abiding covenant ethics continuous into the church, so care for the vulnerable remains a standing obligation, with Matthew 23:23 confirming Jesus retains the same triad (three-part set) as the law's weightier matters.

Even on a strict church-versus-Israel division, James 1:27 supplies a New Testament epistolary (letter-form) command that defines acceptable 'religion' (threskeia) as caring for orphans and widows, and Matthew 23:23 endorses 'justice' (krisis) and 'mercy' (eleos) as binding under the law Jesus addresses, grounding the duty for the present age independent of how the Old Testament prophets are read.

Treats the Old Testament justice demands as fulfilled and reissued in the law of Christ, with James restating the care obligation and Matthew 23:23 anchoring it in Jesus's own teaching, so the duty holds under the new covenant ethic.

A defensible minority lens grants the word-level duty but distinguishes it from any specific political or economic program. The words 'justice' (mishpat), 'mercy' (chesed), 'justice' (krisis), 'mercy' (eleos), and 'to visit/look after' (episkeptesthai) predicate active care on the believing community; they do not, at the word-meaning level, mandate or forbid any one civil mechanism for delivering that care. The duty is decisive in the words. The contested zone is application, the route from text to policy, which the vocabulary does not by itself rank.

hermeneutics.notes: All three continuity frameworks converge on affirmation because the New Testament gospel and letter (Matthew 23:23, James 1:27) carry the duty independently, so the verdict does not depend on resolving the continuity debate. A separate scope-of-application lens is recorded fairly because the word-meaning layer establishes the duty but does not by itself fix the political mechanism for fulfilling it, and that scope distinction is where readers honestly diverge.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Is active care for the poor, the orphan, the widow, and the oppressed presented in the lexical (word-meaning) record as obligatory conduct for God's people?
stem_audit.notes: Two preloading concerns. First, the word 'duty' is a verdict-leaning frame, neutralized above to ask whether the texts present the care as obligatory rather than optional. Second, and more significant, the metadata pairs the social-concern proposition with the Galatians 1:6-9 'curse-on-a-different-gospel' passage (the anathema-on-different-euangelion passage). That coupling can preload the inference that social concern is constitutive of the gospel (euangelion) itself, such that failing it would fall under the 'curse' (anathema). The lexical (word-meaning) evidence does not support that inference: Galatians 1:6-9 is about the content of the preached gospel (euangelion), not ethics, so it is recorded as a neutral, off-target complicating text. The duty verdict is derived only from the command and definitional grammar of Micah 6:8, Isaiah 1:17, Amos 5:24, Matthew 23:23, and James 1:27, and is rendered on the original stem. VERDICT-CHANGED: no.

lay_summary: Across the Bible the words used for caring for the poor, the orphan, the widow, and the oppressed sit in grammatical slots that mark required conduct, not optional kindness. In Micah 6:8 the verse opens by stating what God requires of a person, then lists doing 'justice' (the Hebrew mishpat), loving 'mercy' (chesed), and walking humbly. The phrase 'to do justice' uses an infinitive (a 'to-do' verb form) that places justice (mishpat) in the slot of obligated action. Isaiah 1:17 piles up commands in the imperative mood (the direct command form): learn to do good, seek justice, correct the oppressed, defend the orphan, plead for the widow. The Hebrew parse marks the verbs as predicates (the action side) and the orphan and widow as the direct objects of those commands, so the grammar itself makes the vulnerable the targets of ordered action. Amos 5:24 commands that 'justice' (mishpat) roll down like waters and 'righteousness' (tsedaqah) like an ever-flowing stream, set against worship God refuses. In the gospel, Jesus tells scrupulous tithers in Matthew 23:23 that they have neglected the weightier matters of the law, naming them justice, mercy, and faithfulness. The Greek words there are 'justice' (krisis) and 'mercy' (eleos), which are the standard renderings of the same Hebrew mishpat and chesed, so Jesus carries the prophetic three-part set forward and explicitly ranks it heavier than ritual exactness. In James 1:27 the Greek defines pure and undefiled 'religion' (threskeia) before God as visiting (episkeptesthai) orphans and widows in their affliction (thlipsis), using a verb of ongoing care. Because this is a definition, the care is built into what acceptable religion means rather than offered as an example. One of the listed anchor passages, Galatians 1:6-9, is about something else. There Paul pronounces a curse (anathema) on anyone who preaches a different gospel (euangelion), using the words for gospel and curse. That passage defends the message that is preached, not the ethics of caring for the poor, so it neither proves nor disproves the care obligation and is set aside as off the topic. Where readers diverge is not whether the duty exists in the words, but at the next step. The vocabulary lays down active care on the community, but it does not by itself rank one civil or political mechanism for delivering that care over another. So the word-meaning layer settles the duty, and the application sits outside what the words alone fix.
